paragraphs.text: This [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) cake comes from [Dali](dali:where-it-is), the prefecture in western Yunnan that lies north of Lincang and well north of the pu’er mountains of Xishuangbanna. The prefecture [grows only a little tea of its own](dali:grown-in-dali), mainly on the Cang mountains and the Wuliang range in Nanjian County. Its name is known in pu’er mostly through [the pressing and trading](dali:tuocha-trade) that grew up there on the old caravan routes.

The cake was made in 2005 and is now twenty-one years old. Its leaf was [fried in a wok to kill the green](sheng:making) but never dried with hot air afterwards. Because of that, some of the leaf’s own activity survived, and that is what has let the tea keep changing since. At this age it is past both lines the trade draws for [aged raw pu’er](sheng:ageing): ten years for some, twenty or more for many. How far it has travelled depends on [where it was kept](sheng:storage), because heat and humidity set the pace. It also depends on [how it was pressed](sheng:pressing), because a tight cake changes more slowly than a loose one.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
